opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of those moments where the hair on the back of your neck stands up. On one level it's almost comically mundane: you type a command, hit enter, and somewhere across the facility a machine the size of a small house spins up. But what it really represented was the gap between the digital world and the physical world collapsing.

For most of my career as a mechanical engineer, controlling industrial equipment meant control panels, operators on the floor, layers of procedures, and a lot of caution, for good reason. These systems keep critical infrastructure running, and if you get it wrong, real things break. So the idea that software, and eventually an AI agent, could reach out and directly operate that equipment was a big conceptual shift.

What struck me most was the realization that the bottleneck was never really the hardware. The chillers, pumps, and cooling towers were already capable of running far more efficiently. What held them back was how they were being controlled: static setpoints, rules of thumb, and human operators who simply can't juggle thousands of variables in real time. Once you can close that loop with software, you can start optimizing continuously, learning from the system, and finding efficiencies no human would think to try.

So that keystroke wasn't just turning on a chiller. To me it was proof that AI could move beyond making recommendations on a screen and actually act in the physical world, safely and reliably. That idea has stayed with me ever since and has shaped a lot of what I've chosen to work on.

fable-5.1.text:
I remember that moment really vividly. We were sitting in the data center with the operations team, and I typed a command on my laptop, and somewhere on the other side of the building this massive industrial chiller, a machine that weighs tons and draws megawatts, spun up. And there was this strange silence in the room because everyone understood what had just happened.

For me, the significance wasn't really about the chiller itself. It was that the boundary between software and the physical world had just dissolved. Up until then, AI had mostly lived inside the computer. It recommended videos, it ranked search results, it classified images. All of that is important, but it stays in the digital realm. This was different. A model had looked at the state of the building, decided that more cooling was needed, and acted on it, and a physical object responded. That's the moment I realized this was a fundamentally new kind of thing.

The second thing I felt, honestly, was the weight of responsibility. A recommendation engine that gets it wrong shows you a bad video. A control system that gets it wrong in a data center can damage equipment, or worse, take down services that millions of people depend on. So there was this mix of excitement and a very sober recognition that we now had to think about safety constraints, fallbacks, and what happens when the model is uncertain, in a way we never had to before.

And the third thing was more of a dawning realization about scale. If a few lines of code can control one chiller in one building, then the same approach can apply to every chiller, every pump, every cooling tower, in every facility. And beyond data centers, it's the same physics in commercial buildings, in industrial plants, in the grid. That was the moment the whole problem space opened up for me. It stopped being a data center project and started being a question about how we operate the built environment.

That made the potential of what we were building feel very real.

It made the potential of software feel very tangible—and it also made the responsibility tangible, because those decisions have real consequences.
